# MIL-STD-882E — Department of Defense Standard Practice: System Safety

> **External, not NASA governance.** Useful for comparison and vocabulary. It never establishes
> what NASA requires, and must not be cited as NASA coverage.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Publisher / owner** | U.S. Department of Defense, Air Force Materiel Command System Safety Office. |
| **Kind** | Standard practice (DoD standard). |
| **Status** | Approved 27 September 2023, superseding the 11 May 2012 edition; this copy incorporates "Change 1" (summary of Change 1 modifications on p.4). Current as of this writing; not independently re-checked here. |
| **Where to get it** | Public: Acquisition Streamlining and Standardization Information System (ASSIST) online database, assist.dla.mil; details page `https://quicksearch.dla.mil/qsDocDetails.aspx?ident_number=36027` (Active). Open to the public; the PDF download is a form on that page rather than a direct link |
| **Binds whom** | "This Standard is approved for use by all Military Departments and Defense Agencies within the Department of Defense (DoD)" (Foreword, p.2). It is a DoD contractual instrument: "When this Standard is required in a solicitation or contract, but no specific task is identified, only Sections 3 and 4 are mandatory" (Scope, p.6). It is not NASA-issued and binds nothing at NASA or JPL on its own. |

**What it is good for, relative to NASA's documents.** It supplies a documented, software-specific hazard-classification method with no direct equivalent in the NASA system-safety handbooks reviewed alongside it (NASA/SP-2010-580, NASA/SP-2014-612): a way to rate a software function's safety criticality by its degree of control over hardware, independent of estimating a probability of failure. Section 4.4 states the reason directly: "Determining the probability of failure of a single software function is difficult at best and cannot be based on historical data. Software is generally application-specific and reliability parameters associated with it cannot be estimated in the same manner as hardware" (§4.4, p.22).

**Key content for AI / machine-learning assurance.** Section 4.4, "Software contribution to system risk" (p.22), requires "another approach... for the assessment of software's contributions to system risk that considers the potential risk severity and the degree of control that software exercises over the hardware." §4.4.1 (p.22) defines the machinery: Table IV, Software Control Categories (degree of control software exercises); Table V, the Software Safety Criticality Matrix, crossing severity (Table I) against control category to assign a Software Criticality Index (SwCI); Table VI, relating SwCI to required Level of Rigor (LOR) tasks. The standard names "software system safety techniques and practices" among the changes introduced in this revision (Summary of Change 1 Modifications, p.4) but does not use the words "artificial intelligence," "machine learning," "autonomy," or "neural" anywhere in the sections reviewed (searched; not a full-document search). The control-category approach is agnostic to *how* a software function was built — it classifies by what the function controls, not by its implementation method (our reading); nothing in the text excludes or specifically addresses a learned/AI-enabled function.

**Nearest NASA counterpart.** `../documents/NASA-SP-2014-612.md` (System Safety Handbook, Vol. 2) explicitly builds on this standard rather than replacing it ("builds upon rather than replaces it," §1.3 of that handbook) — the NASA volume adds the Risk-Informed Safety Case (RISC) argument structure on top of a hazard-classification approach of this general kind, but does not reproduce MIL-STD-882E's specific software-control-category/SwCI machinery (our reading; not independently verified against NASA/SP-2014-612's full text for this comparison).
